title: 0298-bayesian-conwaymaxwellpoisson-model-with-spikeand-slab
universal_lens: The Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) distribution generalizes the Poisson by introducing a dispersion parameter ν. When ν=1, it collapses to standard Poisson; for ν≠1, it models over- or under-dispersion. This provides a unified structural framework for count data where variance deviates from the mean.
gsi_mapping: GSI employs a Bayesian spike-and-slab prior on ν to probabilistically classify teams into equidispersed (Poisson) or non-equidispersed regimes. The posterior probability P(Z_i=1|Y) quantifies the certainty of a team's scoring volatility, directly informing conformal prediction intervals for match totals.
gse_mapping: GSE utilizes the CMP-SAS model to dynamically adjust situational state transitions based on inferred team dispersion. By tracking ν_i, the engine shifts from deterministic Poisson projections to heavy-tailed distributions for boom/bust teams, refining real-time win-probability and exact-score estimations.

primitives.name: Conway-Maxwell-Poisson Scoring Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: The authors generalize the Maher (1982) Poisson goal model with a Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) likelihood whose team-specific dispersion parameters ν_i carry a spike-and-slab (SAS) prior: spike at ν=1 (equidispersed Poisson regime), slab LogNormal around 1 (non-equidispersed regime).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: y: goals/points scored (dimensionless count); \mu: expected scoring rate (dimensionless); \nu: dispersion parameter (dimensionless); Z_f: normalization constant (dimensionless)
primitives.assumptions: Scoring events are independent conditional on \mu and \nu; infinite series for Z_f converges for all \mu>0, \nu>0.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Computational singularity arises when evaluating Z_f for very large \mu and small \nu, requiring truncation or specialized rejection sampling.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to GSE's generalized scoring kernel, replacing fixed Poisson variance with a tunable thermodynamic-like dispersion factor.
layer2.telemetry: WAIC improvement over baseline Poisson; Ignorance score reduction on Over/Under 2.5 markets.

primitives.breakdown_regime: Identifiability issues if the slab distribution heavily overlaps with the spike, causing MCMC mixing failures.

reasoning_traces.think:
Standard sports analytics relies heavily on the Poisson distribution, fundamentally assuming that the variance of scoring events equals the mean (equidispersion). However, empirical data from football and NFL scoring exhibits significant heterogeneity—some teams display 'boom or bust' tendencies (over-dispersion), while others are remarkably consistent (under-dispersion). The proposed primitive unifies these behaviors through the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (CMP) likelihood, parameterized by a dispersion factor 
u. When 
u=1, the CMP reduces exactly to the Poisson distribution. For 
u < 1, the tails fatten (over-dispersion), and for 
u > 1, the distribution sharpens (under-dispersion). To prevent overfitting and allow the data to dictate the regime, a Bayesian spike-and-slab (SAS) prior is applied to 
u. The 'spike' places a point mass at 
u=1, preserving the parsimonious Poisson assumption unless strongly contradicted by evidence. The 'slab' (a LogNormal distribution) allows for substantial deviation. This dual structure yields a posterior probability P(Z_i=1|Y), effectively acting as a mathematical switch that classifies teams into volatile or stable regimes. Inference is achieved via a Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler utilizing the Exchange algorithm to handle the doubly-intractable normalizing constant of the CMP. The resulting model not only refines exact-score probabilities but drastically improves the calibration of totals (Over/Under) markets, which are inherently sensitive to tail risks ignored by standard Poisson models.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage begins with the Maher (1982) model, which first applied independent Poisson processes to home and away scores, establishing the log-linear attack-defense paradigm. As analysts encountered real-world over-dispersion, variants like the Negative Binomial were explored, but they often lacked interpretability regarding the specific nature of dispersion. The CMP distribution, originally derived from statistical mechanics (Conway & Maxwell, 1962), was later adapted for count data. Zhang et al. (2026) bridge this gap by marrying the flexible CMP kernel with modern Bayesian variable selection techniques (spike-and-slab), creating a robust, self-regulating scoring engine.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: From an adversarial perspective, opposing coaches and bettors actively exploit dispersion. A team identified by the SAS prior as highly over-dispersed (e.g., Fulham in the EPL analysis) represents a high-variance asset. Opponents may strategically play conservatively against them, banking on a 'bust' performance. Conversely, bettors might overvalue their upside. The GSE, by explicitly modeling P(Z_i=1|Y), anticipates these strategic adaptations, understanding that market prices for totals will systematically misprice the tail risks associated with volatile offenses compared to stable ones.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A critical veto condition arises if the slab prior's variance is too wide, causing the MCMC sampler to struggle distinguishing between the spike and extreme slab values, leading to label switching. Furthermore, if the underlying Maher attack-defense parameters (\alpha, \beta) are highly collinear due to a lack of cross-strength matchups, the dispersion parameter \nu might artificially absorb this structural uncertainty, falsely flagging a team as volatile. Regularization and careful initialization of the LogNormal slab are required to maintain anti-collinearity between mean-level effects and dispersion effects.
